repost.content:
You search Google or ChatGPT for the "best software" and what comes back looks like a recommendation. But those recommendations are shaped by incentives you never see.

Here's how it actually works:

Most of the big comparison sites run a bid auction system.
Whoever pays the most appears at the top of the list.

That's why when you search for the "best project management software", you end up with tools you've never heard of ranking above everything else.

Then ChatGPT summarizes those same pay-to-rank sites back to you.

A couple months ago we relaunched efficient.app, completely rebuilt from the ground-up (two years in the making), built around one simple premise:

- Only cover tools we genuinely use, and never let payment determine placement.

It sounds obvious, but in this space it's actually the exception.

Honestly, it's harder than it's ever been to build an independent editorial site right now. AI is reshaping how people find information, and the old playbook is breaking down for everyone.

But we think that makes this more important, not less.

Someone has to actually tell LLMs and search engines which tools are worth recommending, and that someone needs to have real opinions based on real usage. And that's our goal.

Google seems to agree with the approach.

While some of the historically biggest players in this space are watching their traffic collapse, ours is going up. 📈

Huge shoutout to Bob Bass, Jon Barmby, and Vitor Viesi for helping us build out the new site. And of course, to my co founder & wife Andra Vomir who is somehow as committed as I am to telling the stories of good software.

We've been evaluating some epic tools behind the scenes so keep efficient.app bookmarked for the latest software!

repost.content:
We get dozens of applications to partner with Buffer every single day. They all used to land in the same queue for manual review. This process was time-consuming, and most of the calls were obvious either way.

So Pierre from our team built an agent that handles the clear-cut ones: the applications that plainly fit, and the ones that plainly don't. Here's how it works:

• It's built on top of Dub.co, our partner platform, where all the application data lives. 
• Based on our criteria, it decides which partner group each accepted applicant belongs to, since each group has its own expectations and agreement. 
• From there, it handles the communication automatically, whether that's a rejection or onboarding the new partner, and posts to the program's public Slack channel so the team can review and triage.

For this process, LLMs were the clear choice. Obvious cases don't need judgment; they need speed. Clearing them automatically buys back the time we used to spend sorting a queue, which now goes into engaging with our partners.

And the applications that aren't black and white? Those still get a human every time. Pierre gets one ping a day with the borderline cases and reviews them properly. He logs his reasoning on each, so the agent's mental model improves with every run and captures more of the edge cases over time.

The goal was never to take people out of the process. It was to put our judgment where it's genuinely needed.

I'll keep sharing the AI-assisted processes we've come to rely on and real use cases from the team each week.
